lead: This unit shows how antennas are combined into arrays, how the common directional antennas are built and sized, and how radio waves travel between them. After it you can find the nulls, maxima and beamwidths of an array, design binomial and Dolph-Chebyshev tapers and steer a phased array, size a Yagi, a log-periodic array, a horn, a dish and a patch, measure gain, pattern and polarization, and plan a sky-wave or line-of-sight link.
about: The unit starts with the array factor of two sources and pattern multiplication, extends it to N-element uniform linear arrays in broadside and end-fire form, and then shapes the pattern with binomial and Dolph-Chebyshev tapers and steers it with a phase step. The same array ideas explain the Yagi-Uda and log-periodic antennas. Aperture antennas follow: horns and slots (with Babinet’s principle), parabolic reflectors fed by horns, and printed patches that are often used as array elements. The last two chapters cover how all these antennas are measured and how the waves they launch travel by ground, sky and space wave.

chapters.idea: The pattern of an array is the element pattern multiplied by an array factor that depends only on spacing and phase.
chapters.depth: Cover two identical isotropic sources and two dipoles. Define array factor AF = 2 cos(ψ/2), where ψ = βd cosθ + α, β = 2π/λ, d is element spacing, θ is the angle from the array axis, and α is the current phase difference. Total field pattern = element factor × AF; power pattern is the square. Find nulls and maxima. Some syllabi call this array factorization or pattern multiplication.

figure.aria: Normalized array factor of two isotropic sources spaced λ/2 with a 90° phase difference; a null at 60° and a maximum at 120°.

chapters.example: Two identical isotropic radiators are spaced d = λ/2 apart and fed with a 90° current phase difference. Find the angle of maximum radiation and the first null, with θ measured from the array axis. ψ = π cosθ + π/2; maximum when ψ = 0 gives θ = 120°; null when ψ = π gives θ = 60°.
chapters.trap: Do not add the powers of the two elements; multiply the field patterns and then square for power. Keep θ measured from one fixed reference, array axis or broadside, not both.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: radiation pattern, dipole pattern, field and power patterns.
chapters.leave: N-element arrays and beamwidth formulas go to chapter 2.

chapters.idea: N equally spaced equal-amplitude elements give a narrow beam; broadside fires at 90° to the array axis, end-fire fires along the axis.
chapters.depth: Use AF = sin(Nψ/2) / [N sin(ψ/2)] with ψ = βd cosθ + α. For broadside set α = 0, main beam at θ = 90°. For ordinary end-fire set α = −βd, main beam at θ = 0°. Nulls occur when Nψ/2 = ±mπ. Discuss first-null beamwidth, half-power beamwidth, grating lobes when d ≥ λ, and the gain rise with N and d. Some syllabi call the enhanced end-fire case Hansen-Woodyard.

figure.aria: Four-element broadside uniform linear array with d = λ/2; main lobe at 90° and first nulls at 60° and 120°.

chapters.example: A 4-element uniform linear array has equal in-phase currents and spacing d = λ/2. Find the main-beam direction, first nulls and first-null beamwidth. Broadside maximum is at θ = 90°. Nulls: Nψ/2 = ±π gives ψ = ±π/2, so π cosθ = ±π/2, θ = 60° and 120°. First-null beamwidth = 60°.
chapters.trap: Use α = 0 for broadside but α = −βd for ordinary end-fire; the sign changes the beam direction. Spacing of one wavelength or more creates grating lobes.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1: two-element array factor and pattern multiplication.
chapters.leave: Amplitude tapering, Chebyshev design and electronic steering go to chapter 3.

chapters.idea: Amplitude tapering trades sidelobe level against beamwidth; adding a progressive phase steers the beam without moving the array.
chapters.depth: Binomial arrays use Pascal-triangle coefficients and have no sidelobes but a wide main beam. Chebyshev (Dolph-Chebyshev) arrays give the minimum beamwidth for a chosen sidelobe level in dB. Phased arrays use a phase shifter per element. With θ measured from broadside, the main beam obeys sinθ₀ = −α/(βd). Discuss grating lobes, beam squint with frequency, and linear phased arrays only.

figure.aria: Four-element phased array: a power divider feeds phase shifters set to 0°, −90°, −180° and −270°, steering the beam to 30° from broadside.

chapters.example: A 4-element phased array has d = λ/2. It must steer its main beam to θ₀ = 30° from broadside. Find the progressive phase shift α between adjacent elements. βd = π, so α = −π sin30° = −π/2 = −90°. Phase shifts are 0°, −90°, −180° and −270°.
chapters.trap: A Chebyshev design does not remove sidelobes; it sets them to a chosen level. Phase steering uses α = −βd sinθ₀, not α = −βd cosθ₀, when θ is from broadside.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2: uniform linear array factor, broadside and end-fire phasing.
chapters.leave: Phase-shifter hardware and feed networks go to Unit 4 and Unit 5; mutual coupling is advanced.

chapters.idea: Yagi-Uda uses one driven element and passive parasitic elements for a compact directional beam; log-periodic arrays scale element sizes to work over a wide band.
chapters.depth: Yagi-Uda: reflector longer than the driven element, directors shorter, spacing about 0.15λ to 0.4λ, gain about 7–15 dBi, narrow bandwidth. Log-periodic dipole array: scaling factor τ, spacing factor σ, active region moves with frequency. Bandwidth ratio B = fmax/fmin and element count N = 1 + lnB/ln(1/τ). Some syllabi call it LPDA. Mention log-periodic tooth antennas in one line.

figure.aria: Log-periodic dipole lengths for τ = 0.9 from 750 mm; the shortest of 12 elements is about 235 mm.

chapters.example: A log-periodic dipole array must cover 200 MHz to 600 MHz. Use τ = 0.9 and a longest dipole of 750 mm. Find the bandwidth ratio, number of elements and shortest dipole. B = 3. N = 1 + ln3/ln(1/0.9) ≈ 12. Shortest dipole = 750 × 0.9¹¹ ≈ 235 mm.
chapters.trap: Do not call the Yagi wideband; its bandwidth is only a few percent. In an LPDA the longest dipole works at the lowest frequency, not the shortest.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2: array factor and directive arrays; Unit 2: half-wave dipole.
chapters.leave: Detailed parasitic-element optimisation and balun design go to advanced texts and Unit 5.

chapters.idea: An aperture antenna radiates from an open surface; a horn is a flared waveguide that feeds free space efficiently, and Babinet's principle links a slot to its complementary dipole.
chapters.depth: Cover uniform and tapered apertures, aperture efficiency ηap, effective area Ae = ηapA, and directivity D = 4πAe/λ². Horn types: E-plane, H-plane, pyramidal, conical and corrugated; flare angle and gain. Babinet's principle: complementary screens give related fields; a slot has the same pattern as its complementary dipole with E and H swapped. Booker relation: Zslot × Zdipole = η₀²/4. Some syllabi call this Babinet's principle for electromagnetic fields.

figure.aria: A waveguide feeds a flared horn; the open aperture radiates a beam into free space.

chapters.example: A pyramidal horn has aperture 10 cm × 8 cm at 10 GHz. Aperture efficiency is 0.5. Find effective area and directivity in dBi. A = 80 cm², Ae = 40 cm², λ = 3 cm. D = 4π × 40/9 = 55.85, so D ≈ 17.5 dBi.
chapters.trap: Use effective area, not physical area, in D = 4πAe/λ². Babinet gives the slot pattern from the dipole but not the same impedance.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: waveguides; Unit 2: effective aperture and directivity.
chapters.leave: Parabolic reflectors go to chapter 6; microstrip patches go to chapter 7.

chapters.idea: A parabolic reflector turns the spherical wave from a feed at its focus into a plane wave, giving high gain and a narrow beam.
chapters.depth: Cover diameter D, focal length f and f/D ratio; prime-focus, Cassegrain and Gregorian feeds; feed at the focus; spillover, taper and blockage; aperture efficiency 50–70%. Gain G = η(πD/λ)² and HPBW ≈ 70λ/D degrees. Mention scanning feed and radomes in one line. Some syllabi call it a dish antenna.

figure.aria: A feed at the focus illuminates the parabolic dish; the reflected wave is plane and forms a narrow beam.

chapters.example: A 3 m parabolic dish operates at 4 GHz with aperture efficiency 0.6. Find gain in dBi and approximate HPBW. λ = 0.075 m, D/λ = 40, G = 0.6(π × 40)² = 9475, so G ≈ 39.8 dBi. HPBW ≈ 70 × 0.075/3 = 1.75°.
chapters.trap: The feed sits at the focus, not at the vertex. Gain uses aperture efficiency; the HPBW formula gives degrees only when λ and D use the same unit.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5: aperture efficiency; Unit 2: gain and beamwidth.
chapters.leave: Radar range use goes to Unit 6; detailed Cassegrain design is advanced.

chapters.idea: A microstrip patch is a resonant metal patch on a grounded dielectric; fringing fields at its edges radiate, making a low-profile narrowband antenna.
chapters.depth: Cover rectangular patch design with the transmission-line model. Width W = c/(2f)√(2/(εr+1)); effective dielectric constant εeff; length L = c/(2f√εeff) − 2ΔL with fringing extension ΔL. Feeds: inset, probe and aperture. Bandwidth is a few percent; patch arrays reuse chapters 2 and 3. Some syllabi add fractal and millimetre-wave 5G patch variants; only a few universities examine fractal design in detail.

figure.aria: A copper patch on a dielectric substrate above a ground plane; fringing fields at the patch edges radiate.

chapters.example: Design a rectangular microstrip patch at 2.4 GHz on εr = 4.4 and h = 1.6 mm. Find W and L with the transmission-line model. W ≈ 38.0 mm; εeff ≈ 4.09; L ≈ 29.4 mm after subtracting the fringing length.
chapters.trap: Do not use λ₀/2 for the patch length; the dielectric slows the wave, so use εeff and subtract the fringing length.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: microstrip lines; Unit 2: antenna parameters.
chapters.leave: Patch feed networks and MMIC integration go to Unit 4; array theory stays in chapters 2 and 3.

chapters.idea: Antenna measurements compare the test antenna with a standard in the far field to find gain, pattern cuts and polarization.
chapters.depth: Cover far-field distance R ≥ 2D²/λ, anechoic chamber and outdoor range, gain-transfer or substitution method, standard gain horn, E-plane and H-plane pattern cuts, and polarization measurements. Polarization: linear and circular, axial ratio, spinning dipole and crossed dipoles. Discuss cable loss and multipath. Some syllabi call this antenna test range measurement.

figure.aria: A signal generator drives the test antenna; a receive antenna in the far field feeds a receiver that records gain and pattern.

chapters.example: At 10 GHz, a test antenna has maximum dimension 0.3 m. Find the minimum far-field distance. A standard gain horn reads −30 dBm and the test antenna reads −25 dBm; the horn gain is 15 dBi. Find the test gain. R = 2 × 0.3²/0.03 = 6 m. Gain difference = +5 dB, so test gain = 20 dBi.
chapters.trap: A measurement inside 2D²/λ is a near-field measurement, not a far-field pattern. Keep the sign of dB differences: higher received power means higher gain.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: gain, pattern and polarization; chapter 6: high-gain dish.
chapters.leave: VSWR, power and network-analyzer measurements go to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Radio waves reach a receiver by ground, sky or space waves; the ionosphere bends HF sky waves back to earth.
chapters.depth: Ground wave: LF and MF, follows the earth, vertical polarization, attenuation with distance. Sky wave: HF, ionospheric refraction. Ionosphere layers D, E, F1 and F2. Critical frequency fc = 9√Nmax with Nmax in electrons/m³; MUF = fc secφ with φ measured from the vertical; skip distance and fading. Space wave: VHF, UHF and SHF, line-of-sight, radio horizon, tropospheric scatter and ducting. Some syllabi call this wave propagation.

figure.aria: Ionospheric layers from F2 down to D; HF sky waves refract mainly in F2, while D absorbs by day.

chapters.example: The critical frequency of an ionospheric layer is 5 MHz. Find the MUF for a ray incident at 60° from the vertical. MUF = fc sec60° = 5 × 2 = 10 MHz.
chapters.trap: MUF is higher than critical frequency; use secφ, not cosφ. Sky wave is not used at VHF/UHF beyond the horizon; that is space-wave territory.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: basic wave propagation and frequency bands.
chapters.leave: Radar propagation and atmospheric attenuation for radar go to Unit 6; detailed ionospheric forecasting is advanced.
